draft.title: Experiments and theory
card: In a chance experiment, the results vary. Two sets of 10 coin tosses can give different numbers of heads.
what we expect from the sample space when outcomes are equally likely. For a fair coin, the chance of heads is 1/2.
the number of times an event happened ÷ the number of trials. If heads came up 7 times in 10 tosses, it is 7/10.
With only a few trials, the relative frequency can be far from the theoretical probability. With many trials, it usually gets closer, but it need not match exactly.
draft.remember: More trials usually bring the relative frequency closer to the theoretical probability.

a.q: Sam tosses a fair coin many times. What is likely to happen to the relative frequency of heads as the number of tosses grows?
opts: It gets closer to 1/2
It gets closer to 1
It becomes exactly 1/2 every time
It moves away from 1/2
a.why: With more trials, the relative frequency usually gets closer to the theoretical probability of 1/2. It is not forced to equal 1/2 exactly, so the option saying it becomes exactly 1/2 every time is wrong.
a.clue: Think about what the theoretical probability of heads is.

b.q: Priya spins a fair spinner with 4 equal sections, one of them red. In 20 spins she gets red 8 times. In 400 spins she gets red 96 times. Which statement is correct?
opts: The 400 spins are closer to the 1/4 theory
The 20 spins are closer to the 1/4 theory
Both are equally close to the 1/4 theory
The 20 spins show the spinner is not fair
b.why: Relative frequency is 8/20 = 0.4 for 20 spins and 96/400 = 0.24 for 400 spins. The theoretical probability is 1/4 = 0.25, so 0.24 is much closer. A result like 0.4 in few trials is not enough to say the spinner is unfair.
b.clue: Turn both results into decimals and compare them with 0.25.

b.best: The 400 spins are closer to the 1/4 theory

proposal.title: Experiments and theory
card: In a chance experiment, the results vary. Two sets of 10 coin tosses can give different numbers of heads.
We can compare the relative frequency from our trials with the theoretical probability. For heads on a fair coin, the theoretical probability is 1/2.
With only a few trials, the relative frequency can be far from the theoretical probability. For example, 10 tosses might give mostly heads. That alone does not show the coin is unfair.
With many trials, the relative frequency usually gets closer to the theoretical probability. It need not match it exactly.
proposal.remember: Few trials can be far off. Many trials usually land close to the theory.

a.q: Sam tosses a fair coin many times. What is likely to happen to the relative frequency of heads as the number of tosses grows?
opts: It gets closer to 1/2
It gets closer to 1
It becomes exactly 1/2 every time
It moves away from 1/2
a.why: With more trials, the relative frequency usually gets closer to the theoretical probability of 1/2. It need not equal 1/2 exactly, so the option saying it becomes exactly 1/2 every time is wrong.
a.clue: Think about what the theoretical probability of heads is.

b.q: Priya spins a fair spinner with 4 equal sections, one red. Her relative frequency of red is 0.4 after 20 spins and 0.24 after 400 spins. Which statement is correct?
opts: The 400 spins are closer to the 1/4 theory
The 20 spins are closer to the 1/4 theory
Both are equally close to the 1/4 theory
The 20 spins show the spinner is not fair
b.why: The theoretical probability is 1/4 = 0.25. The 400 spins give 0.24, only 0.01 away, while the 20 spins give 0.4, which is 0.15 away. A result far off in a few trials is not enough to say the spinner is unfair.
b.clue: Compare each result with 1/4 written as a decimal.

final.title: Experiments and theory
card: In a chance experiment, the results vary. Two sets of 10 coin tosses can give different numbers of heads.
We can compare the relative frequency from our trials with the theoretical probability. For heads on a fair coin, the theoretical probability is \(\frac{1}{2}\).
With only a few trials, the relative frequency can be far from the theoretical probability. For example, 10 tosses might give mostly heads. That alone does not show the coin is unfair.
With many trials, the relative frequency usually gets closer to the theoretical probability. It need not match it exactly.
final.remember: Few trials can be far off. Many trials usually land close to the theory.

It gets closer to 1

It moves away from \(\frac{1}{2}\)
a.why: With more trials, the relative frequency usually gets closer to the theoretical probability of \(\frac{1}{2}\). It need not equal \(\frac{1}{2}\) exactly, so the option saying it becomes exactly \(\frac{1}{2}\) every time is wrong.

b.q: Priya spins a fair spinner with 4 equal sections, one red. Her relative frequency of red is 0.4 after 20 spins and 0.24 after 400 spins. Which statement is correct?
opts: The 400 spins are closer to the \(\frac{1}{4}\) theory
The 20 spins are closer to the \(\frac{1}{4}\) theory
Both are equally close to the \(\frac{1}{4}\) theory
The 20 spins show the spinner is not fair
